source_title: Trespass with an Unmanned Aircraft System
regulated_activity: Causing a UAS to cross a property line and come within 50 ft of a dwelling to coerce/intimidate/harass, or after notice to desist for any other reason; or taking off/landing in violation of FAA special security instructions or security-sensitive airspace restrictions
requirement_type: Prohibition (misdemeanor), with consent and FAA-authorization exceptions
summary: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 711-1114, added by Act 58 (2023), makes it a misdemeanor to intentionally cause a UAS to cross the property line of another and come within 50 ft of a dwelling to coerce, intimidate, or harass another person, or — after having been given actual notice to desist — for any other reason at all; or to take off or land a UAS in violation of current FAA special security instructions or UAS security-sensitive airspace restrictions. The section does not apply where consent to entry was given by a person with legal authority to consent (or a person lawfully present on the property), or where the operator was authorized by federal regulations and operated the UAS lawfully and consistent with those regulations.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not fly within 50 ft of a dwelling across a property line for any purpose once the property owner or occupant has given actual notice to desist -- the statute's 'for any other reason at all' clause means continued proximity flights after notice are a likely violation even for routine survey/inspection work, regardless of harassment intent. Obtain documented consent before any low-altitude work near occupied dwellings outside the project boundary, and confirm the flight does not implicate current FAA special security instructions or security-sensitive airspace restrictions.

source_title: Misuse of Uncrewed Aircraft (First, Second, and Third Degree)
regulated_activity: First degree: arming a UAS with a firearm/explosive/electric gun/weapon of mass destruction, interfering with a manned aircraft, delivering prison contraband, or causing serious bodily injury. Second degree: disabling Remote ID transmission, defeating/failing to operate required anti-collision lighting, causing substantial bodily injury, or causing more than $20,000 property damage. Third degree: tampering with a registration number, obstructing a police officer/firefighter, causing bodily injury, causing more than $750 damage, or operating while impaired
summary: Act 161 (2024), effective July 2, 2024, created a graduated three-tier felony framework for UAS misuse. Misuse of uncrewed aircraft in the first degree (§ 711-1121) is a Class A felony covering arming a drone with a firearm, explosive, electric gun, or weapon of mass destruction; interfering with or disrupting a manned aircraft; delivering contraband, drugs, or dangerous instruments into a prison; or causing serious bodily injury. Misuse in the second degree (§ 711-1122) is a Class B felony covering disabling a drone's Remote ID transmission, defeating or failing to operate required anti-collision lighting, causing substantial bodily injury, or causing more than $20,000 in property damage. Misuse in the third degree (§ 711-1123) is a Class C felony covering tampering with a registration number, obstructing a police officer or firefighter, causing bodily injury, causing more than $750 in damage, or operating under the influence. An earlier (~2015) provision separately made it unlawful to install or carry weapons aboard a UAS used for commercial purposes flown across or above the State; its exact current codified citation was not independently confirmed and it may now substantially overlap with § 711-1121's weaponization felony.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Add this restriction to the state preflight screen, brief the field crew on the prohibited conduct, and identify a stop-work or escalation point. Document any exception relied upon rather than assuming Part 107 authority resolves the state requirement.

verification_status: Existence, tier structure, effective date, and covered conduct re-corroborated in this retrofit pass via multiple independent secondary legal-summary sources describing Act 161 (consistent in every material detail with the original pass's findings: three graduated felony tiers, Remote ID/anti-collision-lighting provisions in the second-degree offense, the $20,000 property-damage threshold, and the contraband-delivery and weaponization provisions in the first-degree offense). A direct fetch of the full statutory text of Sections 711-1121 through 711-1123 was attempted again in this pass against both the official capitol.hawaii.gov HRS pages and Justia's codification; both returned no retrievable content, the same result as the original pass. Confidence held at Moderate pending a successful direct full-text read.
notes: The Remote ID and anti-collision lighting provisions in section 711-1122 (second-degree, Class B felony) are directly relevant to routine AEC commercial operations -- equipment malfunction or misconfiguration causing a Remote ID or anti-collision lighting failure could carry felony exposure in Hawaii in a way most other states treat as a lesser (or no) offense. Recommend direct verification of the full statutory text (e.g., via a Hawaii Legislative Reference Bureau session-law PDF for Act 161) before advising a client on the precise elements and any available defenses; two independent research passes have now been unable to retrieve the verbatim codified text through standard web-fetch tools.

source_title: Violation of Privacy (Second and First Degree)
regulated_activity: Installing or using a device, including a drone, to observe, record, or broadcast a person in a private place without consent; recording showing the person nude or engaged in sexual activity
requirement_type: Prohibition (misdemeanor, elevated to felony for aggravated conduct)
summary: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 711-1111 (violation of privacy in the second degree) makes it unlawful to install or use a device — including a drone — to observe, record, or broadcast a person in a 'private place' (somewhere a person may reasonably expect to be safe from casual or hostile intrusion) without consent; a basic violation is a misdemeanor (up to 1 year imprisonment, up to a $2,000 fine). Where the recording shows the person nude or engaged in sexual activity, § 711-1110.9 (violation of privacy in the first degree) applies instead, a Class C felony punishable by up to 5 years imprisonment and a $10,000 fine.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Design acquisition and data-handling workflows to minimize unnecessary capture of people and private activity. Confirm the source-supported consent or project-purpose basis before flight and carry that limitation through processing, access control, retention, and delivery.

geographic_scope: Statewide (DLNR-managed conservation, natural, and cultural resource lands)
issuing_authority: Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources (DLNR), Division of Conservation and Resources Enforcement (DOCARE)
source_title: DLNR Unmanned Aircraft Systems Program (DOCARE Conservation Enforcement) and Covered-Foreign-Entity UAS Procurement Restriction
citation: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 199-9 (enacted 2023, DLNR program-establishment deadline June 30, 2025)
source_type: Binding law or regulation; official agency policy
effective_date: 2023 (enactment); program required to be established by June 30, 2025
uas_topic: State-agency UAS enforcement program; UAS procurement/foreign-hardware restriction
regulated_party: DLNR / DOCARE conservation and resources enforcement officers (program authorization); DLNR itself (procurement restriction)
regulated_activity: DOCARE's use of UAS to monitor, investigate, and obtain evidence of natural- and cultural-resource violations; DLNR's purchase, operation, or acquisition of UAS equipment
requirement_type: Agency program authorization and mandatory reporting; procurement prohibition with a case-by-case waiver
permit_or_approval_required: N/A for private operators; internal DLNR/DOCARE program governs agency use
commercial_operator_relevance: Low for private operators; Moderate for AEC firms performing conservation-adjacent work for or near DLNR
summary: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 199-9 required DLNR to establish an unmanned aircraft systems program, compliant with applicable federal and state law, to assist DOCARE in carrying out its conservation and resources enforcement duties, with the program required to be established by June 30, 2025. Conservation and resources enforcement officers may use UAS to monitor, investigate, and obtain evidence of natural- and cultural-resource violations. DLNR must maintain detailed records of UAS use and program effectiveness and submit an annual report to the legislature (first due no later than January 1, 2026, and annually thereafter). Separately, and of direct relevance to state-agency UAS procurement, the statute prohibits DLNR from purchasing, operating, or otherwise acquiring or using UAS manufactured or assembled by a 'covered foreign entity' (the same category of entity targeted by the federal American Security Drone Act and DJI/Autel-style state procurement bans elsewhere), and bars state funds -- including funds awarded through a contract, grant, or cooperative agreement -- from being used by DLNR in connection with such UAS, subject to a case-by-case waiver by the chairperson of the Board of Land and Natural Resources for counter-UAS activities, criminal investigative purposes, or exigent circumstances. This fills a category (state-agency UAS procurement/foreign-hardware restriction) that has been absent in most other states retrofitted to date.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This program governs DOCARE's own enforcement UAS use rather than private commercial operators directly, but AEC firms performing conservation-area mapping, habitat assessment, or resource-inventory work for or adjacent to DLNR should expect DOCARE UAS activity to be present in the same areas and should coordinate mission timing accordingly. If an AEC firm is contracted to supply or operate UAS on DLNR's behalf, confirm the equipment is not manufactured or assembled by a covered foreign entity (e.g., certain Chinese manufacturers) before proposing a fleet, since DLNR cannot lawfully purchase, operate, or fund such equipment absent a waiver.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Any DLNR contract, grant, or cooperative agreement involving UAS equipment or services should confirm compliance with the covered-foreign-entity procurement restriction before funds are committed; a waiver from the chairperson of the Board of Land and Natural Resources is available only for counter-UAS activities, criminal investigative purposes, or exigent circumstances, not as a general cost-saving measure.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Screen any UAS platform proposed for DLNR/DOCARE work against the federal covered-foreign-entity list before quoting a fleet; this operates the same way as the federal American Security Drone Act restriction and similar state-level bans (e.g., Texas's Prohibited Technologies List) and should be treated as a hard procurement gate rather than a preference.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Confirm current DLNR/DOCARE UAS-program policy and the January 2026 (and subsequent annual) legislative report directly with DLNR before advising a client on the program's current operational scope; the underlying statute is binding but the program's day-to-day implementation details are set by DLNR policy rather than the statute's own text.
verification_status: Substance confirmed via multiple independent web-search-mediated readings of Justia's codification of Haw. Rev. Stat. section 199-9 in this retrofit pass, consistently corroborating the program-establishment deadline, DOCARE's authorized UAS uses, the annual reporting requirement, and the covered-foreign-entity procurement and funding restriction with its narrow waiver.
